name: Pas-ta'ai (Short Spirit Ceremony)
domain: Saisiyat tribal ceremony, spirit appeasement, reconciliation
description: After nightfall, a bright chiming rises through the valley — the sound of the "hip bells" (taba'ang), back ornaments studded with small copper bells that ring all night long in time with the dancers' steps. This is the Saisiyat Pas-ta'ai, the Short Spirit Ceremony (also called Pasta'ai), one of the most strictly regulated of all ceremonies among Taiwan's indigenous peoples. It is not a rite of blessing but one of consolation — held to appease the spirits of the legendary Short People (Ta'ai), who once taught the Saisiyat how to farm yet were killed by the tribe through treachery, leaving behind a dying curse. To calm the anger of the Short Spirits and pray for the peace of the community, the Saisiyat hold a minor ceremony every two years and a grand ceremony every ten, each lasting four days and three nights. The singing and dancing carry on from sunset until sunrise, the mood solemn and hushed, filled with awe and remorse toward the Short Spirits.
story: Long ago, the Saisiyat and the short-statured Ta'ai lived as neighbors across a river. The Ta'ai were skilled in farming and in magic, and they taught the Saisiyat how to cultivate the land; for a time the two peoples were close. But the Ta'ai repeatedly offended the women of the Saisiyat, and at last, unable to bear it any longer, the tribe laid a trap and drowned nearly all of them in the river — only two survived. The survivors did not seek revenge. Instead they left a curse — that the Saisiyat would suffer failed harvests and misfortune — and yet they also taught the people, line by line, the songs and the rules of a ceremony to be held every year in search of forgiveness, before turning and departing forever. From that day the Saisiyat have kept the Pas-ta'ai, generation after generation. There is no victor in this story; it remembers instead a debt of gratitude, a wrong that was done, and the remorse a people take upon themselves through a whole night of singing and dancing.
worship: The Pas-ta'ai is wholly unlike an ordinary blessing ceremony — there is no incense and no idol; its heart is "atonement" and "reconciliation," the people speaking directly to the Short Spirits through song, dance, and ritual. The whole ceremony is strictly divided into six stages: Informing the Spirits, Welcoming the Spirits, Entertaining the Spirits, Sending Off the Spirits, Mud-Smearing, and Purification in the River. Participants must observe many taboos — no quarreling while the ceremony lasts, no weapons carried onto the ritual ground, and clothing kept chiefly to white and red. Each Saisiyat clan holds its own duty: the Zhu clan leads the rites, the Feng clan keeps the ceremonial songs, the Zhao clan bears the ritual flag — a reflection of the tribe's social order. The hip bells are the most important of the ritual instruments; each clan's bells carry their own patterns, handed down through the generations and never to be copied at will. The cycle of more than fifteen ceremonial songs, each with its fixed order and meaning, takes a whole night to sing through in full.
festivals: The Pas-ta'ai is held in mid-October of the lunar calendar (approximately November-December on the solar calendar), simultaneously at two ritual grounds: the Southern Group in Xiangtianhu, Nanzhuang Township, Miaoli County, and the Northern Group in Daai, Wufeng Township, Hsinchu County. The minor ceremony spans four days and three nights, while the grand ceremony (every ten years) extends to six days and five nights with even greater scale. The first night is "Welcoming the Spirits," with all tribespeople lined up as the lead elder chants the welcoming song. The second and third nights are "Entertaining the Spirits," as participants dance in large circles throughout the night, hip bells chiming and songs echoing through the mountain valleys — spectacular and solemn. The final morning is "Sending Off the Spirits" — the most sorrowful moment — as the tribe sings farewell songs, watching the Short Spirits depart. Designated a National Important Folk Custom, the ceremony is open to outside observers but with strict viewing rules (no black clothing, no unauthorized photography), reminding visitors to respect the Saisiyat people's reverence for the Short Spirits.

temples.name: Xiangtianhu Ritual Ground
temples.deityStory: The primary ritual ground for the Southern Group of the Pas-ta'ai ceremony.

temples.name: Wufeng Ritual Ground
temples.deityStory: The primary ritual ground for the Northern Group of the Pas-ta'ai ceremony.

name: Alizu (Ancestral Spirit)
domain: Siraya Ancestral Spirit, tribal guardian, rain prayer, healing
description: Step into a Siraya kuwa — a public ritual house — and you will find no idol at all, only a pot wrapped in red cloth, quietly holding water: this is Alizu (also called Ali-Mu or Taizu). Alizu is the most revered ancestral spirit of the plains-dwelling Siraya people, and unlike the sculpted deities of the Han, has no fixed form; the spirit is represented instead by pots, bottles, and jars filled with water — a practice known as 'pot worship.' The pot is bound in red cloth, and the water within, called 'Xiang Water,' is believed to heal, to drive off evil, and to bring blessing. The kuwa is not only a center of belief but the place where the community gathers to deliberate. The most important Siraya rite of the year is the 'Night Ceremony' on the fourteenth day of the tenth lunar month, when the people offer betel nut and rice wine and, hand in hand, circle and sing the ancient 'Qian Qu' (holding-hands songs) in gratitude for the ancestral spirits' protection.
story: Alizu is not a single deity but the Siraya people's collective name for their ancestral spirits — spirits who watch over the community's cycles of birth, aging, sickness, and death, and who move with the rhythms of the natural world. Dutch rule and the wave of sinicization under the Qing dealt heavy blows to Siraya tradition, and their language, their surnames, and their ways of life were changed piece by piece — yet pot worship stubbornly endured, becoming the most vivid marker of Siraya identity. Among the most famous beliefs passed down through the generations is that of the healing 'Xiang Water' — the pot water blessed by Alizu, said to cure any illness. The 'General Pillar' within the kuwa stands for the authority and power of the ancestral spirits. To this day, places such as Danei, Jiali, and Dongshan in Tainan still keep their kuwa and Night Ceremony traditions intact, so that the life of this Austronesian ancestral faith carries on in the Qian Qu songs sung through the night.

temples.name: Tainan Danei Toushe Kuwa
temples.deityStory: Toushe Kuwa is the largest and most well-preserved center for the Siraya Night Ceremony. It enshrines the Five Ancestral Sisters. The structure is divided into three chambers, symbolizing different ranks of spirits. The annual Night Ceremony attracts numerous visitors and scholars, witnessing the revitalization of Siraya culture.

temples.name: Jiali Beitouyang Lichang Temple
temples.deityStory: Beitouyang was the homeland of the Soulangh community of the Siraya tribe. Lichang Temple worships Alizu, preserving traditional pot worship and Xiang Water rituals. The Night Ceremony here combines traditional chanting with modern cultural activities to promote Siraya heritage.

associatedTemples: Tainan Danei Toushe Kuwa (Danei District, Tainan City)
Jiali Beitouyang Lichang Temple (Jiali District, Tainan City)
worship: Alizu worship differs entirely from the temple practices of the Han, preserving the original ritual character of the Austronesian peoples: the place of worship is the kuwa, not a temple, and the sacred symbol is a water-filled ritual pot, not a statue. In the rite, the people offer betel nut, rice wine, and tobacco, and the ceremony is led by the "Ang-i," a female priestess. The Ang-i holds a place of great weight in Siraya society — she can commune with the ancestral spirits, heal the sick, and divine fortune. At the heart of it all is the "Xiang Water," the pot water blessed by Alizu, believed to heal and to ward off evil; and in matters great and small, the people come to the kuwa to seek Alizu's counsel. Notably, the faith is passed down through the female line and the kuwa is kept by female elders — an echo of the matrilineal society of the early Siraya.
festivals: The most important Siraya ceremony is the "Night Ceremony" (Mahanru), held annually on the 14th-15th of the 10th lunar month. Beginning at nightfall and lasting until dawn, the entire ceremony is led by the Ang-i as tribespeople sing the ancient "Qian Qu" (Holding Hands Songs), forming large circles hand-in-hand while invoking ancestral spirits. The "Pig Flipping" ritual — turning a whole pig as a sacrificial offering — is the Night Ceremony's most iconic image. The Tainan Danei Toushe Kuwa hosts the grandest Night Ceremony, attracting thousands annually and designated as a Tainan Municipal Folk Custom. Dongshan Jibeiwa and Zuozhen Kousheliao also maintain Night Ceremony traditions. Some Siraya communities also hold a smaller "Spring Ceremony" in the 3rd lunar month to thank ancestral spirits for a good spring planting.

name: Paiwan Hundred Pacer Snake Belief
domain: Guardian of the chiefly lineage, protector of the tribe, symbol of nobility and courage
description: On the door lintels of Paiwan slate houses, in their wood carvings, clay pots, and finest ceremonial dress, the same figure appears again and again — the coiled Hundred Pacer Snake (Vulung). In the culture of the Paiwan and Rukai peoples, the Hundred Pacer holds the highest place of honor, revered as an embodiment of the ancestors and a guardian spirit. The Paiwan believe their forebears share an inseparable kinship with the snake: it is the guardian of the chiefly families and the spiritual emblem of the whole tribe. For this reason its diamond-patterned motif spreads across clothing, carving, architecture, and everyday objects — the single most central cultural symbol of the Paiwan, and not merely a design but an entire people's memory of where they came from.
story: In the Paiwan creation story, the Sun laid two eggs atop the sacred Mount Kavulungan (Dawushan): from one hatched the Hundred Pacer Snake, and from the other emerged the first ancestor of the Paiwan people. And so the snake and the Paiwan are siblings, and it guards the people as it would its own kin. Another legend tells of a chief's daughter who fell in love with a Hundred Pacer that had taken the form of a young man; the two married and bore the descendants of the chiefly line — which is why only chiefly families hold the right to use the snake motif. In the strict Paiwan social hierarchy, the emblem marks noble status and may not be used by commoners. And out of this kin-like reverence, when the people meet a Hundred Pacer in the mountains they will never harm it; instead they respectfully give it a wide berth, and some offer millet wine and betel nut — for in their eyes it is not a snake, but a kinsman come from afar.

temples.name: Mount Kavulungan (Sacred Mountain)
temples.deityStory: Mount Kavulungan (Dawushan) is the sacred mountain of both the Paiwan and Rukai peoples, believed to be the dwelling place of ancestral spirits. The Paiwan hold that after death, the soul returns to Mount Kavulungan to reunite with the Hundred Pacer Snake ancestor spirit. Many important ceremonies are oriented toward this sacred peak.

worship: Paiwan reverence for the Hundred Pacer Snake is woven into every important moment of daily life. At tribal ceremonies or great family occasions, the chief prays to the Hundred Pacer ancestral spirit with offerings of millet wine, betel nut, and game meat. When a new slate house is to be raised, the snake motif is carved into its pillars to call down the ancestral spirits' protection over the home. At a wedding, the bride wears traditional dress embroidered with the Hundred Pacer pattern — a patterning that signifies she is receiving the blessing of the ancestral spirits. For the Paiwan, the Hundred Pacer dwells not in some distant heaven but on the pillars of the house, on the clothes they wear, and in every moment that calls for protection.
festivals: The most significant Paiwan ceremony is the Five-Year Ceremony (Maleveq), also known as the Covenant Between Humans and Spirits. Held once every five years over a period of roughly two weeks, the ceremony's purpose is to welcome the ancestral spirits back to the community for a reunion with the living. The climactic moment is the bamboo pole ball-piercing ritual: a shaman throws a rattan ball high into the air, and warriors attempt to pierce it with long bamboo poles. Those who succeed are believed to have received a special blessing from the ancestors. The Five-Year Ceremony has been designated a National Important Folk Custom of Taiwan.

name: Tayal Ancestral Spirit Belief (Utux)
domain: Guardian of the people, upholder of social order, moral and ethical guide
description: For the Tayal, there is an invisible measure for how a person should live and act, and its name is "gaga." At the heart of Tayal belief stand two interconnected words — "Utux," the ancestral spirits, and "gaga," the teachings and norms of the ancestors. The Utux are the souls of the departed forebears, and the Tayal believe the ancestral spirits keep watch over their descendants without ceasing; the will of the spirits is passed down through gaga — a body of traditional law spanning morality, social custom, and ritual taboo, guiding how one should live and how one should treat others. Those who keep gaga receive the protection of the ancestral spirits; those who break it face their reckoning. Gaga is written on no paper — it lives in the words and deeds of every Tayal.
story: The Tayal creation story runs like this: in the earliest age, a great boulder on the sacred Mount Papak Waqa (present-day Dabajianshan) split open, and from the fissure walked the first man and the first woman — the ancestors of the Tayal. These ancestors taught their descendants to hunt, to weave, and to farm, and set down gaga for the people to live by. The best-known of all Tayal traditions is facial tattooing (ptasan): a man had to prove the courage of the headhunt and a woman her mastery of weaving before earning the tattoo that marked adulthood and honor. Yet its meaning reaches beyond this life — the Tayal believe that after death the soul walks toward the Rainbow Bridge (Hongu Utux), and at its far end lies the land of the ancestral spirits. The spirits stand guard upon the bridge, and only those souls who kept gaga all their lives and earned their tattoos may cross to be reunited with their ancestors. The mark upon the face thus becomes a pass into the realm of the spirits.

temples.name: Mount Papak Waqa (Sacred Mountain)
temples.deityStory: Mount Papak Waqa (Dabajianshan) is the sacred mountain of the Tayal people, regarded as the birthplace of their entire nation. The Tayal believe their ancestors emerged from a great boulder on this mountain. It holds the highest spiritual significance, and Tayal people offer prayers of reverence when facing the sacred peak.

associatedTemples: Mount Papak Waqa (Jianshi Township, Hsinchu County / Tai'an Township, Miaoli County)
worship: Tayal worship centers on prayer to the ancestral spirits. There are no fixed temples; the rites are held in the community's gathering house, or out in the mountains and the natural world itself. The offerings must include millet wine, together with game — pork, or muntjac and other quarry — and millet cakes made of glutinous rice. During the rite, the tribal elders lead the people in prayer to the ancestral spirits, laying the community's affairs, great and small, before the Utux and seeking their guidance and protection. This is not a plea addressed to gods, but something closer to descendants speaking quietly with the ancestors who have watched over them all along.
festivals: The most important Tayal ceremony is the Thanksgiving Ritual (Smyus), held after the millet harvest. The entire community gathers as elders lead offerings of the newly harvested millet to the ancestral spirits, expressing gratitude for their protection throughout the year. The celebration includes traditional singing and dancing, jaw harp performances, and communal circle dances. The Ancestral Spirit Ceremony (Maho) is another vital observance dedicated to honoring departed ancestors, during which the community offers millet wine and other provisions to maintain their spiritual bond with those who came before.

name: Bunun Sky God Belief (Dihanin)
domain: Ruler of heaven and earth, grantor of bountiful harvests, patron of the legendary sun-shooting hero
description: When the Bunun look up at the moon, they read in it not only its waxing and waning but the whole year's calendar — when to sow, when to weed, when to harvest, and which ceremony must be held. Bunun belief takes "Dihanin" — the Sky God, or Heaven — as its highest spiritual power, holding sway over all things between heaven and earth: the weather, the growth of the crops, and even the fate of human beings. Of all Taiwan's indigenous peoples, the Bunun place the greatest weight on calendar and agricultural ritual: from the phases of the moon they worked out a precise farming calendar, each month carrying its own ceremonies and taboos, interlocking into a complete belief system built around the cultivation of millet. The Sky God is not far away — it is present in every full moon and every furrow of the millet field.
story: The most celebrated Bunun legend is the tale of Shooting the Sun. In the earliest age, two suns took turns lighting the earth, and their blazing heat dried up the rivers, scorched the crops, and left the people in misery. A warrior of the tribe resolved to take his young son and walk toward the place where the suns rose, to shoot one down. Father and son crossed range after range and walked so long that the orange seed the father had idly planted on the day they set out had grown into a great tree. At last, reaching the edge of the sky, the warrior drew his bow and struck one of the suns. The wounded sun bled, staining the heavens fiery red — and this, the Bunun say, is the origin of the sunset glow; the injured sun slowly dimmed until it became the moon we know today. From then on one sun and one moon shared the sky, and the earth came back to life. Seeing the courage of the Bunun warrior, Dihanin gave the people the seeds of millet and taught them to farm, so that the Bunun would never go hungry again.

temples.name: Jade Mountain (Sacred Mountain)
temples.location: Nantou County / Chiayi County / Kaohsiung City
temples.deityStory: Jade Mountain (Yushan) stands at the heart of the Bunun people's traditional territory, regarded as the place closest to the Sky God Dihanin. Important Bunun ceremonies are oriented toward Jade Mountain as the community prays for divine protection. The Bunun are the highest-dwelling indigenous people in Taiwan, having lived alongside the high mountains for generations.

associatedTemples: Jade Mountain (Nantou County / Chiayi County / Kaohsiung City)
worship: Bunun offerings are chiefly millet wine and game meat, with tribal elders or ritual specialists leading the people in prayer to the Sky God Dihanin. The Bunun possess a unique "painted calendar" — pictographic symbols recording each month's farming tasks and ceremonies, which makes them the only indigenous people in Taiwan to have developed a form of written record. But the most unforgettable element of their worship is the Pasibutbut (Eight-Part Polyphony): the people form a circle and, with harmonies layered one upon another, sing out the prayer for a bountiful millet harvest. It is no performance, but a whole community giving voice, as one, to its wish before the Sky God.
festivals: The most important Bunun ceremony is the Ear-Shooting Festival (Malahtangia), held annually in April or May. The festival serves as both a coming-of-age rite and a hunting ceremony for Bunun men, who must shoot deer ears hung on a wooden rack to demonstrate their marksmanship. During the festival, participants perform the internationally celebrated Pasibutbut (Eight-Part Polyphony) — also known as the "Prayer for a Bountiful Millet Harvest." Using a distinctive vocal technique in which singers produce layered harmonies, the performance creates an otherworldly sound that rises as a prayer to Dihanin. In 1952, Japanese musicologist Kurosawa Takatomo sent a recording of this singing to UNESCO, where it astonished the international music community and has since been hailed as one of the great treasures of human musical heritage.

name: Tao Ocean Spirit Belief (Anito)
domain: Ocean guardian, bestower of flying fish, protector against malevolent spirits
description: Each spring, shoals of flying fish migrate to the waters off Orchid Island, and the whole year's rhythm of Tao life sets off with them. The Tao people (also called Yami) live on Orchid Island (Lanyu) and are the only indigenous people of Taiwan whose culture is centered on the ocean. Their belief revolves around "Anito" (souls or spirits), holding that all things possess a spiritual essence. Among these beliefs, the customs and rites bound up with the flying fish form the most distinctive chapter of Tao culture — the flying fish is regarded as sacred food bestowed by the heavenly spirits, and around its catching, its eating, and its taboos an entire rigorous code of custom has grown up. For the Tao, how they treat these fish is how they keep faith with the sea and with the ancestors.
story: The Tao legend of the flying fish begins like this: in ancient times the people did not yet know how to tell one fish from another, and cooked flying fish together with other kinds, so that one after another they fell ill. One night the Flying Fish Spirit — a black-winged flying fish — came in a dream to an elder and told him that flying fish were a sacred gift the heavenly spirits had given especially to the Tao, and that they must be cooked in dedicated pots, never mixed with other fish. The spirit patiently taught the elder the ways of catching flying fish, the rules for eating them, and the many taboos to be observed. When the elder awoke, he passed these teachings on to his people one by one, and from that time the Tao built an entire culture around the flying fish. When one may fish and when one must stop, how the catch is preserved and shared out — this whole body of rules governing the flying-fish season became the cornerstone of Tao social order.

temples.name: Orchid Island Communities
temples.deityStory: Orchid Island's six communities — Yayo, Iratay, Imourud, Iraralay, Iranumilk, and Ivalino — each maintain their own boat houses and ceremonial grounds. The Tao have no permanent temples; rituals take place on the shore, in boat houses, or on the community gathering grounds. The Ivalino (Yehyin) community preserves the most intact cluster of traditional semi-subterranean houses, offering a vital window into Tao cultural heritage.

associatedTemples: Orchid Island community ceremonial grounds (Lanyu Township, Taitung County)
worship: Tao worship takes place not in temples but in close bond with the sea and the natural world. Before the flying-fish season, the men gather at the shore for the Fish-Summoning Ceremony, casting chicken blood upon the waves to call the flying fish in. When a new plank boat is ready to launch, the people slaughter pigs and chickens and anoint the hull with their blood, praying for a safe voyage and an abundant catch. The Tao also keep strict food taboos — men and women eat different species of fish, and elders and children each have fish they may or may not eat. These seemingly elaborate rules are how the people carry their reverence for the sea into every meal and every venture out onto the water.
festivals: The Flying Fish Festival is the central ceremony of Tao life, unfolding in three seasonal phases. In spring, the Summoning Ceremony (mivanwa) takes place: men don traditional loincloths and silver helmets and gather at the shore to call the flying fish through chanting and dance. In summer, the Preservation Ceremony marks the drying and storing of the catch. In autumn, the Final Eating Ceremony closes the flying fish season — any fish remaining uneaten must be discarded and may no longer be consumed. The Boat Launching Ceremony (manawag) is another major occasion. The Tao plank boat (tatala) is hand-built from multiple types of wood by the community, its hull painted in the traditional colors of red, white, and black. The launching ceremony is both grand and deeply sacred.

name: Puyuma Ancestral Spirit Belief (Palakuwan)
domain: Guardian of tribal youth, preserver of cultural knowledge, upholder of social order
description: In a traditional Puyuma settlement, the unmarried boys leave home to live in a hall called the "Palakuwan" — living, learning, and honoring the ancestral spirits together. This is the core of the Puyuma (Pinuyumayan) traditional belief system: the worship of ancestral spirits. The Palakuwan is far more than a building — it is the living vehicle of Puyuma ancestral belief, of the age-grade organization, and of cultural transmission. And it differs fundamentally from Han belief: here there is no ranking of "god" above "human." The ancestors are not lofty deities but "forerunners" still bound up with the life of the community, whose wisdom, whose rules, and whose protection are passed to the descendants through the rites of the Palakuwan. The Puyuma live chiefly in Beinan Township and Taitung City, and it is the Nanwang settlement (Puyuma) that preserves the culture most completely — its year-end ceremony (Mangamangayau) standing as the emblem of the whole people's cultural inheritance.
story: A Puyuma boy's coming of age is walked, step by step, inside the Palakuwan. Traditional Puyuma society kept a strict age-grade organization: a male passed from child (Trakubakuban) to boy (Mialalravar), youth (Maradawan), young man (Bangsaran), and at last adult (Maizang), each grade carrying its own duties and responsibilities within the hall. There the elders passed on, by word of mouth, the stories of the ancestors, the history of the community, and the skills of living to the next generation. In Puyuma belief the ancestral spirits dwell not only within the settlement but among the mountains, the rivers, and the land — the return of game and the abundance of the harvest alike are seen as the spirits' blessing. This transmission once came close to breaking: the Japanese "kominka" policy pressed down on indigenous tradition, and after the war, as Christianity and Catholicism reached the settlements, many families converted. Yet the heart of it — the Palakuwan and the year-end ceremony — did not vanish, for the people guarded it. After the 1980s, as the indigenous rights movement rose, Puyuma youth set about systematically reviving the halls and the year-end ceremony; the Nanwang ceremony, brought back after decades of interruption, became one of the defining stories of indigenous cultural revival in Taiwan.

temples.name: Nanwang Community (Puyuma)
temples.deityStory: Nanwang is the largest Puyuma community and maintains the most complete gathering hall system and ceremonial traditions. The community's youth gathering hall remains active to this day, with the annual Grand Hunting Ritual and Monkey Ritual drawing community members home from across the island. Nanwang is also renowned for its rich musical culture, having produced several celebrated singers.

temples.name: Jhihben Community (Katipul)
temples.deityStory: Jhihben is another major Puyuma community, distinguished by its "Born from Bamboo" origin narrative. The community has a particularly rich tradition of shamanism, with female shamans continuing to practice healing ceremonies that have been passed down through the generations — making it an important site for the study of indigenous spiritual practices in Taiwan.

worship: Puyuma ancestral worship is a wholly different matter from the temple practices of the Han. The traditional Palakuwan is a men-only space, and outsiders — women and non-members above all — may not enter freely. Worship centers on oral recitation, chanting, prayer, and offering: the elders (Maizang) report the community's affairs to the ancestral spirits in the Puyuma tongue, ask their protection, and give thanks for their blessing, while the offerings are mostly betel nut, rice wine, homemade clay-pot wine, game, and crops — an expression of the spirit of "sharing everyday life with the ancestors." Some settlements today open certain areas to outside observers during the year-end ceremony, but this openness comes with conditions: visitors must obtain the community's prior consent, observe the dress code, refrain from photographing particular rites, withhold careless comment, and follow the guidance of the people. In the end, the first lesson in understanding Puyuma culture is to respect this people's standing as the authors of their own culture.
festivals: The grandest Puyuma ceremony is the Grand Hunting Ritual (Mangayaw), held at the end of December each year and lasting approximately one week. All men of the community — from adolescents to elders — enter the mountains by age group to hunt, testing their skills and presenting the year's accomplishments to the ancestral spirits. The Youth Monkey Ritual (Mangamangayangayam) takes place just before the Grand Hunting Ritual: young men must use bamboo bows and arrows to shoot at monkey-shaped targets (real monkeys are no longer used), and only those who pass this test are eligible to participate in the Grand Hunting Ritual, marking their pivotal transition from boyhood to manhood. Together, these two ceremonies are known as the Year-End Rites and have been designated a National Important Folk Custom of Taiwan.
